sources.title: There's a reason your child wants to read the same book over and over again
sources.quote: A preference for familiarity, rather than novelty, is commonly reported at young ages. ... Repetition aids learning complex information by increasing opportunities for the information to be encoded. ... Being read the same story four times rather than two times improved 1.5- and two-year olds’ accuracy. ... Repeated readings of the same storybook also help children learn novel words. ... Younger children take longer to learn new information than older children, and they also forget it faster.
sources.supports: Young children often prefer the familiar; repetition gives more chances to encode information; toddlers read a story four times rather than two were more accurate; repeated readings help children learn new words; younger children forget faster. Studies cited are mostly with toddlers and young preschoolers, applied here to ages 3 to 5 as an analogy.

sources.title: Why Children Like Repetition, and How It Helps Them Learn
sources.publisher: Psychology Today, The Baby Scientist (Vanessa LoBue, Ph.D., Rutgers University-Newark), 10 Jul 2019
sources.quote: An early developing preference for the familiar is actually quite common in infancy and early childhood. ... children learned new words better when they heard them in one story repeated three times than when the same words appeared across three different stories (3-year-olds; Horst, Parsons, & Bryan, 2011). ... babies who were read a storybook four times imitated the demonstrated actions more than babies read it twice (18 to 24 months; Simcock & DeLoache, 2008). ... this extra practice might be just what children need to learn new things.
sources.supports: A preference for the familiar is common in early childhood; 3-year-olds learned new words better from one story heard three times than from three different stories; toddlers read a story four times imitated more actions than those read it twice. The article summarises studies and is a blog by a university psychologist.

sources.title: Why do kids love reading the same book over and over?
sources.publisher: Popular Science (Sarah Lindenfeld Hall), 11 Jun 2025, quoting developmental psychologist Aliza Pressman and Vanderbilt professor Deborah Wells Rowe
sources.quote: Young children thrive on structure. ... routines give kids a dependable framework that helps them feel more secure, confident, and in control (Pressman). ... Whenever a kid is seeking comfort and control and safety (Pressman). ... They're gaining confidence in themselves as understanders and, eventually, as readers (Rowe).
sources.supports: Experts quoted say routines give children a dependable framework that helps them feel secure and in control, and that repeated reading builds confidence as understanders and eventually readers. That a repeated story is part of a routine is our reading of the article.

sources.title: How to Deal With Reading the Same Book 100 Times
sources.quote: Read in funny accents. ... Explain to your toddler that the book wants to hear a new story. ... Find books with the same character or by the same author and illustrator. ... Read two books at bedtime. Parent chooses one, child chooses the other. ... You read a new book and have them read you their old favorite. ... Realize that in 20 years, this book will be one that you associate with your children and cherish.
sources.supports: A parenting article with six practical tips for coping with a child who wants the same book repeatedly. It is practical advice, not research.

sources.title: Why do kids love reading the same book over and over?
sources.publisher: Popular Science (Sarah Lindenfeld Hall), 11 Jun 2025, quoting developmental psychologist Aliza Pressman and Vanderbilt professor Deborah Wells Rowe
sources.quote: Young children thrive on structure. ... routines give kids a dependable framework that helps them feel more secure, confident, and in control (Pressman). ... Whenever a kid is seeking comfort and control and safety (Pressman). ... They're gaining confidence in themselves as understanders and, eventually, as readers (Rowe).
sources.supports: Experts quoted say routines give children a dependable framework that helps them feel secure and in control, and that repeated reading builds confidence as understanders and eventually readers. That a repeated story is part of a routine is our reading of the article.

sources.title: There's a reason your child wants to read the same book over and over again
sources.quote: A preference for familiarity, rather than novelty, is commonly reported at young ages. ... Repetition aids learning complex information by increasing opportunities for the information to be encoded. ... Being read the same story four times rather than two times improved 1.5- and two-year olds’ accuracy. ... Repeated readings of the same storybook also help children learn novel words. ... Younger children take longer to learn new information than older children, and they also forget it faster.
sources.supports: Young children often prefer the familiar; repetition gives more chances to encode information; toddlers read a story four times rather than two were more accurate; repeated readings help children learn new words; younger children forget faster. Studies cited are mostly with toddlers and young preschoolers, applied here to ages 3 to 5 as an analogy.

sources.title: How to Deal With Reading the Same Book 100 Times
sources.quote: Read in funny accents. ... Explain to your toddler that the book wants to hear a new story. ... Find books with the same character or by the same author and illustrator. ... Read two books at bedtime. Parent chooses one, child chooses the other. ... You read a new book and have them read you their old favorite. ... Realize that in 20 years, this book will be one that you associate with your children and cherish.
sources.supports: A parenting article with six practical tips for coping with a child who wants the same book repeatedly. It is practical advice, not research.

sources.title: Why do kids love reading the same book over and over?
sources.publisher: Popular Science (Sarah Lindenfeld Hall), 11 Jun 2025, quoting developmental psychologist Aliza Pressman and Vanderbilt professor Deborah Wells Rowe
sources.quote: Young children thrive on structure. ... routines give kids a dependable framework that helps them feel more secure, confident, and in control (Pressman). ... Whenever a kid is seeking comfort and control and safety (Pressman). ... They're gaining confidence in themselves as understanders and, eventually, as readers (Rowe).
sources.supports: Experts quoted say routines give children a dependable framework that helps them feel secure and in control, and that repeated reading builds confidence as understanders and eventually readers. That a repeated story is part of a routine is our reading of the article.

sources.title: There's a reason your child wants to read the same book over and over again
sources.quote: A preference for familiarity, rather than novelty, is commonly reported at young ages. ... Repetition aids learning complex information by increasing opportunities for the information to be encoded. ... Being read the same story four times rather than two times improved 1.5- and two-year olds’ accuracy. ... Repeated readings of the same storybook also help children learn novel words. ... Younger children take longer to learn new information than older children, and they also forget it faster.
sources.supports: Young children often prefer the familiar; repetition gives more chances to encode information; toddlers read a story four times rather than two were more accurate; repeated readings help children learn new words; younger children forget faster. Studies cited are mostly with toddlers and young preschoolers, applied here to ages 3 to 5 as an analogy.
